body:
Fuels used for cooking and transport

A fuel is a substance that releases useful energy when it burns. Many domestic and vehicle fuels are hydrocarbons, which are compounds made only of carbon and hydrogen. When these fuels burn in sufficient oxygen, they release heat and form mainly carbon dioxide and water vapour.

Petroleum and natural gas are important sources of hydrocarbon fuels. They are called fossil fuels because they formed from the remains of ancient organisms over millions of years. They are non-renewable on the human timescale.

PNG, LPG and CNG are commonly used gaseous fuels, but their names refer to different fuel compositions or methods of supply and storage. In particular, PNG and LPG are not the same fuel.

PNG: Piped Natural Gas

PNG stands for Piped Natural Gas. It is natural gas supplied to consumers through a network of pipelines, commonly for cooking and heating.

Natural gas consists mainly of methane (CH4), the simplest hydrocarbon. It may also contain smaller amounts of other gases, including ethane. The exact composition varies with the source and treatment of the gas.

In a domestic PNG connection, gas reaches the premises through a pipeline network. A meter records consumption, and the household uses a suitable gas stove or other approved appliance. The consumer does not need to replace an LPG cylinder when the gas is exhausted because the supply comes through the pipeline.

The word piped describes the method of delivery. PNG is not a special chemical substance different from natural gas.

LPG: Liquefied Petroleum Gas

LPG stands for Liquefied Petroleum Gas. It consists mainly of propane (C3H8) and butane (C4H10), in proportions that may vary.

Propane and butane can be stored as liquids under moderate pressure. Therefore, a relatively large quantity of LPG can be kept in a portable cylinder. When the cylinder valve is opened and the fuel passes through the regulator, LPG is supplied to the stove as a gas and burns at the burner.

LPG is obtained during petroleum refining and natural gas processing. Its portability makes it useful in places where a piped-gas network is unavailable.

Comparison of PNG and LPG

FeaturePNGLPG
Full formPiped Natural GasLiquefied Petroleum Gas
Main constituentMethanePropane and butane
Common domestic supplyPipeline networkPressurised cylinder
Fuel in domestic supplyGasStored as liquid; supplied to burner as gas
Relative density after leakageLighter than airHeavier than air
Common applicationCooking and heatingCooking and heating

CNG: Natural gas stored under pressure

CNG stands for Compressed Natural Gas. It is natural gas, mainly methane, compressed to high pressure for storage. It is widely used as a fuel in suitably equipped vehicles, including cars, buses and autorickshaws.

PNG and CNG generally use the same principal fuel, natural gas. Their important distinction is how that gas is supplied or stored. PNG travels through pipelines to consumers, whereas CNG is kept in high-pressure cylinders, especially in vehicles.

Compression is not liquefaction. CNG remains a compressed gas in its normal vehicle storage system. By contrast, LPG is stored principally as a liquid under pressure. These differences also explain why fuel-specific equipment is necessary.

Remember the three names: PNG describes natural gas delivered by pipe; CNG describes natural gas stored by compression; LPG describes a propane–butane fuel stored in liquefied form.

Leakage, safety and correct appliances

Natural gas is lighter than air under ordinary conditions. A PNG or CNG leak therefore tends to rise and disperse upwards where ventilation permits. LPG vapour is heavier than air and can collect near the floor or in low-lying, poorly ventilated spaces. Both fuels are highly flammable, so neither characteristic makes a leak harmless.

Natural gas and LPG are normally given a noticeable warning odour so that leaks are easier to detect. If a leak is suspected, the gas supply should be shut off where it is safe to do so, the area ventilated and the authorised gas provider contacted. Flames and electrical switches should not be operated in the affected area.

Appliances designed for LPG and PNG are not automatically interchangeable. Their fuel characteristics and supply conditions differ; any required conversion must be carried out by authorised personnel.

Why these fuels matter in Gujarat

City gas distribution networks supply natural gas for domestic, commercial and transport uses in parts of Gujarat. Vadodara is a longstanding example of piped natural gas use, also identified in school-level science material. Gujarat therefore provides a practical example of the difference between domestic PNG supply and vehicle CNG supply.

Although natural gas and LPG generally burn with less smoke than traditional solid domestic fuels, they are still combustible carbon-containing fuels. Their use does not mean that carbon dioxide emissions become zero.

Prelims focus

  • PNG: Piped Natural Gas; its main constituent is methane, CH4.
  • LPG: Liquefied Petroleum Gas; it contains mainly propane and butane.
  • CNG: Compressed Natural Gas; it is primarily methane stored at high pressure.
  • PNG and CNG are natural-gas applications; LPG has a different principal composition.
  • Natural gas is lighter than air, while LPG vapour is heavier than air.
  • Trap: PNG is not a mixture of propane and butane, and CNG is not ordinarily stored as a liquid.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Coal and Petroleum, sections 5.2–5.4, printed pp. 59–62, 2018–19 edition; Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board, FAQs for PNG, questions on PNG composition, supply and comparison with LPG, pp. 1–2, consulted 3 November 2026; Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell, Frequently Asked Questions, Natural Gas, questions 1–5, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: PNG, LPG and CNG: Composition, Supply and Safe Use

body:
What is ethanol-blended petrol?

Petrol is a liquid fuel obtained mainly from petroleum. It contains a mixture of hydrocarbons and is commonly used in spark-ignition engines. Ethanol is a different substance: an alcohol with the chemical formula C2H5OH.

Ethanol can be produced from biological raw materials containing sugars or starch. Sugarcane-derived materials, including molasses, and suitable food grains such as maize are among the feedstocks used in India. Because this ethanol originates from recently grown biomass, it is classified as a biofuel.

Under the Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme, fuel-grade ethanol is mixed with petrol. The number following the letter E indicates the nominal percentage of ethanol in the fuel blend by volume.

E20 means petrol containing 20% ethanol and 80% petrol by volume. Similarly, E10 contains 10% ethanol and 90% petrol by volume.

Understanding E20 with a simple example

Consider 100 litres of finished E20 fuel. Its nominal composition is 20 litres of ethanol and 80 litres of petrol. It is neither pure ethanol nor a blend containing 20% petrol. The letter E refers specifically to ethanol, not to methanol or diesel.

Ethanol contains oxygen within its molecules. This makes it an oxygen-containing fuel component, which can influence the combustion of petrol. However, a more oxygenated fuel does not automatically eliminate all exhaust pollutants.

Why does India blend ethanol with petrol?

India uses ethanol blending for several connected purposes.

  • Reducing petroleum dependence: Replacing a part of petrol with domestically produced ethanol reduces the amount of petroleum-derived fuel needed for the same volume of blended petrol.
  • Supporting domestic agriculture and industry: Ethanol creates a market for eligible agricultural feedstocks and associated processing industries.
  • Promoting a renewable fuel component: Ethanol produced from biomass can be replenished through new agricultural production, unlike fossil petroleum.
  • Improving some fuel characteristics: Ethanol has a high octane rating, which helps resist abnormal knocking in appropriately designed petrol engines.

Environmental benefits must be understood carefully. The overall greenhouse-gas effect of producing and using ethanol depends on its feedstock, farming practices, processing energy and transport. At the vehicle's exhaust, burning E20 still produces carbon dioxide and may produce other pollutants. Therefore, E20 is not a zero-emission fuel.

India's policy and blending progress

The National Policy on Biofuels, 2018, amended in 2022, advanced the target of 20% ethanol blending in petrol from 2030 to Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2025–26. An ethanol supply year runs from 1 November to 31 October.

The 2022 amendment expanded the permitted feedstock framework and supported the wider availability of biofuels. The EBP Programme is implemented through oil marketing companies supplying ethanol-blended petrol.

In an official statement dated 23 July 2026, the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas reported the following average blending levels:

Ethanol Supply YearAverage ethanol blendingData status
2022–23About 12%Reported yearly average
2023–24About 14.6%Reported yearly average
2024–25About 19.2%Reported yearly average
2025–2620%Reported average for November 2025–June 2026

These figures establish the progress reported by the Government as of 23 July 2026. In particular, the 20% figure for 2025–26 covered November 2025 to June 2026; it must not be misread as a newly verified final average for the entire supply year.

At the stated content cutoff of 3 November 2026, the 23 July 2026 government release remains the dated source used here for these specific progress figures. That release stated that no decision had been taken to increase the nationwide base ethanol blend beyond 20%.

E20, engine compatibility and fuel economy

Vehicle engines and fuel systems are designed to work with specified fuels. E20-compatible petrol vehicles are intended to operate on petrol containing up to the specified ethanol blend. Vehicle owners should follow their manufacturer's fuel recommendations.

Ethanol has a lower energy content per litre than petrol. As a result, changes in fuel economy are possible, particularly in vehicles originally designed for a lower ethanol blend. The actual difference depends on vehicle design, engine calibration, driving conditions and maintenance. A numerical difference in the energy content of pure ethanol and petrol cannot simply be treated as the percentage loss of vehicle mileage with E20.

In its 23 July 2026 statement, the Government reported that testing and manufacturer service records had not established widespread engine failures attributable to E20. It also stated that some vehicles designed for E10 could experience a limited reduction in fuel economy. The correct conclusion is that fuel economy and compatibility depend on the vehicle; neither universal damage nor identical mileage for every vehicle should be assumed.

How is E85 different?

E85 contains 85% ethanol and 15% petrol by volume. The Government identified it as a separate fuel for specifically designed and certified flex-fuel vehicles. Its availability does not mean that ordinary nationwide petrol has changed from E20 to E85.

Prelims focus

  • E20 contains 20% ethanol and 80% petrol by volume.
  • Ethanol is an alcohol with the formula C2H5OH
  • The National Policy on Biofuels was introduced in 2018 and amended in 2022.
  • The 2022 amendment advanced the 20% blending target from 2030 to ESY 2025–26.
  • The Government reported 20% average blending for November 2025–June 2026 in its 23 July 2026 statement.
  • Trap: E20 is neither pure ethanol nor an emission-free fuel. E85 is a different blend intended for suitable flex-fuel vehicles.

[Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, National Policy on Biofuels, 2018, Amendment Notification dated 15 June 2022, provisions on blending targets and feedstocks, consulted 3 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Ethanol Blending in India, factsheet dated 5 July 2026, sections on policy evolution and fuel characteristics, consulted 3 November 2026; Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Government Highlights Safety, Performance and National Benefits of Ethanol-Blended Petrol, Press Information Bureau release ID 2288271, 23 July 2026, blending table and sections on E20, E85 and fuel economy, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: E20 Petrol and India's Ethanol Blending Programme

body:
Why does burning fuel produce exhaust gases?

Most conventional motor vehicles obtain energy by burning fuel with oxygen inside an engine. This chemical process is called combustion. The energy released moves the vehicle, while the substances formed during the reaction leave through the exhaust system.

Hydrocarbon fuels contain carbon and hydrogen. When combustion is complete, the carbon is converted mainly into carbon dioxide (CO2) and the hydrogen into water (H2O).

Real vehicle engines do not always achieve perfectly complete combustion. The amount of available oxygen, the mixing of fuel and air, temperature and engine condition can influence the products released. Some important pollutants arise from incomplete combustion; others form because of the high temperatures reached during burning.

Complete and incomplete combustion

Complete combustion

When sufficient oxygen is available and the fuel burns effectively, a hydrocarbon produces mainly carbon dioxide and water vapour. Carbon dioxide is generally not the main cause of immediate poisoning from vehicle exhaust at ordinary outdoor concentrations, but it is an important greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change.

Incomplete combustion

When combustion is incomplete, some carbon-containing fuel may form carbon monoxide (CO), unburnt hydrocarbons or soot instead of being completely converted into carbon dioxide.

  • Carbon monoxide: A colourless, odourless and poisonous gas. It enters the blood and binds strongly to haemoglobin, reducing the blood's ability to carry oxygen.
  • Unburnt hydrocarbons: Fuel-related organic compounds that escape without complete combustion. Some contribute to the formation of ground-level ozone in the presence of other pollutants and sunlight.
  • Soot and smoke: Fine particles associated with incomplete combustion, especially visible in poorly maintained diesel engines and other combustion sources. Inhaled particles can affect the respiratory system.

CO and CO2 must not be confused. Carbon monoxide is particularly dangerous because it interferes with oxygen transport in the blood. Carbon dioxide is a major greenhouse gas and is a normal product of complete hydrocarbon combustion.

Why does a vehicle produce nitrogen oxides?

Air contains about 78% nitrogen and about 21% oxygen by volume. Nitrogen gas, N2, is ordinarily relatively unreactive. However, the high temperatures produced during engine combustion can cause nitrogen and oxygen to react, forming nitrogen oxides.

These pollutants are commonly called NOx. The most important members for basic vehicle-emission studies are nitric oxide (NO) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2). Nitric oxide released by an engine can undergo further reactions in air and form nitrogen dioxide.

NOx is therefore different from carbon monoxide and unburnt hydrocarbons: it does not arise merely because carbon-containing fuel has failed to burn completely. It is closely related to high-temperature combustion and atmospheric chemical reactions.

How exhaust pollutants differ

SubstancePrincipal formation or sourceMain concern
COIncomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuelReduces blood oxygen transport
CO2Complete combustion of carbon-containing fuelGreenhouse effect and climate change
Unburnt hydrocarbonsFuel escaping complete combustionAir pollution and ozone formation
Smoke and sootIncomplete combustion and particle formationRespiratory harm and reduced visibility
NOxHigh-temperature reactions involving nitrogen and oxygenRespiratory irritation, ozone, particles and acid rain

What determines whether a fuel is cleaner?

The amount and type of exhaust pollution depend on both the fuel and the vehicle. Engine condition, maintenance, driving conditions and emission-control equipment also matter. Changing to a cleaner-burning fuel can reduce certain pollutants, but it does not guarantee that every type of emission will disappear.

Natural gas generally produces less soot than traditional solid fuels and can have favourable emissions characteristics when compared with some petrol or diesel applications. Nevertheless, a CNG vehicle still burns a carbon-containing fuel. It releases carbon dioxide and may produce nitrogen oxides.

E20 petrol contains a renewable ethanol component, but the remaining petrol and the combustion process still produce exhaust gases. Similarly, a petrol vehicle in good condition can emit carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons, although suitable emission-control equipment can reduce them.

Role of a catalytic converter

A catalytic converter is an exhaust-treatment device fitted to many petrol vehicles. Its catalysts help convert harmful gases into less harmful products. In a suitable system, carbon monoxide is converted into carbon dioxide, unburnt hydrocarbons are converted mainly into carbon dioxide and water, and nitrogen oxides are reduced mainly to nitrogen gas.

A catalytic converter reduces pollutants; it does not make the exhaust completely harmless or eliminate carbon dioxide. Its effectiveness also depends on proper vehicle operation and maintenance.

Prelims focus

  • Complete hydrocarbon combustion produces mainly CO2 and H2O.
  • Incomplete combustion can produce poisonous CO, unburnt hydrocarbons and soot.
  • CO reduces oxygen transport by binding to haemoglobin.
  • NOx commonly refers to nitric oxide and nitrogen dioxide in vehicle-emission discussions.
  • High-temperature combustion can form NOx from nitrogen and oxygen.
  • Trap: Cleaner-burning fuel does not mean zero CO2 or zero NOx emissions.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Combustion and Flame, sections 6.1 and 6.6, printed pp. 64–74, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Pollution of Air and Water, sections 18.1–18.3, printed pp. 239–242, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Natural Resources, section 14.1.4, Air Pollution; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Environmental Issues, section 16.1, Air Pollution and Its Control.]
title: Vehicle Combustion and the Main Exhaust Pollutants
